slides.headline: A royal family portrait full of secrets.
slides.sub: Francisco Goya, The Family of Charles IV, 1800-01

slides.headline: The royals
slides.text: Madrid, 1800. Goya paints the whole Spanish royal family, life size. It looks like a grand official portrait. But look closer.

slides.headline: The queen
slides.text: Queen Maria Luisa stands in the centre, not the king. Many at court believed she was the one who really ruled Spain.

slides.headline: The king
slides.text: King Charles IV stands to one side, covered in medals, looking pleased with himself. He loved hunting more than ruling.

slides.headline: The youngest
slides.text: The queen holds the hand of her youngest son. At court, people whispered about who his real father was.

slides.headline: No face
slides.text: Near the heir, a young woman turns her face away. Many think she stands for his future bride, not yet chosen.

slides.headline: The painter
slides.text: And in the shadows on the left, Goya painted himself at his easel, watching them, just like Velázquez in Las Meninas.

slides.headline: Flattery?
slides.text: A later writer joked they look like a baker and his wife after winning the lottery. Yet the royals seem to have liked it.

slides.headline: Your verdict
slides.text: Goya flattered no one, and the royals didn't seem to notice. Was he quietly mocking them, or just telling the truth?
